Historical Rainfall across Singapore (2017–2024)

Spark-based Weather-Pattern Analysis, Rainfall Prediction, and a Model × Compute Benchmark

Dataset: data.gov.sg collection 2279 — Historical Rainfall across Singapore (National Environment Agency), annual datasets 2017–2024, 5-minute rainfall (mm).

1. Introduction

This project processes and models Singapore's five-minute rainfall records (2017–2024) using Apache Spark (PySpark). It delivers the two required tasks and an additional benchmarking study:

  • Task 1 — Explore weather patterns: how rainfall varies within a year (seasonal and daily cycles) and across 2017–2024, with spatial analysis.
  • Task 2 — Predict rainfall: a Spark MLlib model estimating the probability a station accumulates more than a given threshold of rain in the next 30 minutes, taking (station, prediction time, threshold) as input.
  • Additional study: the prediction task run across 8 models (6 Spark MLlib + 2 PyTorch deep models on GPU) and 5 compute configurations (single-process Spark, two Spark Standalone cluster layouts, two Dockerized Spark clusters), comparing predictive error against training/prediction time.

2. Computing environment

All work was performed on a single laptop (no cloud/HPC). The pipeline is written so the same code runs across several Spark deployment modes by reading the master and executor/driver resources from environment variables (src/spark_utils.py).

Component Specification
Host Laptop, 32 GB RAM, Windows + WSL2 (Ubuntu)
WSL2 allocation 24 GB RAM, 16 logical cores, 8 GB swap
Python / Java Python 3.12, OpenJDK 21
Spark PySpark 3.5.3 (local[*] and Spark Standalone)
GPU NVIDIA RTX 3050 Ti Laptop, 4 GB VRAM (CUDA 12.4, PyTorch 2.6)
Containers Docker 29.7.2 + Compose v5.5.0

Compute configurations used in the benchmark (§6):

Config Spark master Total cores Notes
local-all local[*] 16 single JVM, all cores
standalone-2x2 spark://localhost:7077 4 2 workers × 2 cores
standalone-4x2 spark://localhost:7077 8 4 workers × 2 cores
docker-2w spark://spark-master:7077 4 2 worker containers
docker-3w spark://spark-master:7077 6 3 worker containers
gpu — (PyTorch) 1 GPU deep models only

The Spark Standalone and Docker "clusters" run their master and workers as separate processes/containers on the one machine — they demonstrate real distributed Spark deployment (network shuffle, separate executor JVMs) but share the same physical hardware.

3. Data cleaning

The eight yearly CSVs (~7.8 GB) are downloaded via the data.gov.sg poll-download API (src/download_data.py) and cleaned into a single Parquet dataset partitioned by year (src/clean_data.py).

Steps and rationale:

  1. Timestamps in Singapore Time (SGT). The Spark session time zone is pinned to Asia/Singapore so every derived calendar feature and the 30-minute label align with the local time the task concerns.
  2. Cast and validate the reading. reading_value → double (mm per 5-min); drop rows with null, negative, or physically impossible values (> 60 mm per 5 min, treated as sensor error).
  3. De-duplicate on (station_id, timestamp), keeping the record with the latest update_timestamp (most recent correction) → exactly one reading per station per 5-minute slot, which is essential for correct rolling sums.
  4. Resolve station identity. Raw names alternate between the real name (e.g. "Alexandra Road") and the bare id (e.g. "S77"); coordinates are stable. We assign one canonical, human-readable name per station_id and take the median latitude/longitude (robust to stray values).
  5. Derive calendar fields (year, month, hour, day-of-week, …) once, reused by both tasks.

Result: 48,538,713 clean readings across 91 stations, 2017–2024. Rainfall is highly sparse — the median 5-minute reading is 0 mm; among wet readings the median is 0.2 mm, the 99th percentile ~6.8 mm, and the 99.9th ~10.6 mm. This sparsity directly shapes the Task 2 modelling (heavy class imbalance → emphasise AUC-PR).

The storage choice (CSV → Parquet, partitioned by year) is deliberate: Parquet is columnar + compressed (far smaller, faster scans) and partition pruning lets Spark read only the years a query needs.

4. Task 1 — Weather patterns

All aggregation is done in Spark (src/task1_explore.py); only small summary tables are collected to the driver for plotting. Because the monitoring network grew over the period (54 stations in 2019 → 80 in 2020), every annual and monthly figure is normalised per station, so comparisons reflect weather, not changing coverage.

4.1 Change across the years (2017–2024)

Mean per-station annual rainfall:

Year 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024
mm 1989 2056 1526 2072 2569 2750 2475 2359
stations 62 56 54 80 76 72 74 70

2019 is markedly the driest year and 2021–2022 the wettest — consistent with Singapore's drier 2019 and wet La-Niña-influenced 2021–22. The overlaid station count shows the totals are normalised, not an artefact of coverage.

4.2 Change within a year (seasonal cycle)

The year-by-month heatmap and the averaged monthly climatology show Singapore's monsoonal structure, with the wetter Northeast-monsoon months (Nov–Jan) and the inter-monsoon peaks:

4.3 Change within a day (diurnal cycle)

Both the mean rainfall intensity and the probability that a 5-minute reading is wet rise sharply to a mid-afternoon peak (≈14:00–16:00 SGT) and fall to an overnight minimum — the classic tropical afternoon-convective pattern. For example the wet-reading fraction climbs from ~1.1% at 23:00 to ~5.8% at 15:00.

The pattern holds across monsoon seasons, with amplitude differences:

4.5 Extreme events

Counting station-days with ≥ 50 mm daily total, heavy-rain frequency peaked in 2021 (875 station-days), matching the wet-year signal. A 2022 daily total near 786 mm stands out as a probable extreme/outlier (flagged, not removed).

Year 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024
station-days ≥50 mm 393 347 263 558 875 740 745 660

Task 1 summary: rainfall in Singapore is dominated by brief, intense afternoon convective events; it varies seasonally with the monsoon regimes, differs across the island spatially, and shows clear interannual swings (dry 2019, wet 2021–22) in both mean totals and heavy-event frequency.

5. Task 2 — Predicting P(rain > threshold in next 30 min)

5.1 Problem framing

The task requires the rainfall threshold to be a user input at prediction time. Instead of training a separate model per threshold, we make the threshold a model feature: for each (station, 5-min timestamp) we emit one labelled example per candidate threshold (0.2, 1, 2, 5, 10 mm), with label 1 if the true next-30-minute accumulation exceeds that threshold. A single model then answers any threshold at prediction time, including unseen values.

5.2 Feature selection (leakage-free)

All features use only information available up to the prediction time (src/task2_features.py):

  • Recent-rainfall context: current 5-min reading, previous reading, rolling 30/60/180-minute sums, and minutes-since-last-rain. (These dominate the signal — rain is strongly autocorrelated at short lead times.)
  • Cyclical time: hour and month encoded as sine/cosine pairs (so hour 23 is adjacent to hour 0, December to January); weekend and NE/SW-monsoon flags.
  • Location/identity: latitude, longitude, and station index.
  • The query threshold (mm).

The label is the sum of the next six 5-minute readings; rows without a complete 30-minute future window are dropped so the label is exact. Feature engineering is materialised once (src/task2_build_features.py) to avoid recomputing the expensive per-station windows on every run.

5.3 Model and evaluation protocol

The graded model is a Gradient-Boosted Trees (GBT) classifier (Spark MLlib) in a Pipeline: StringIndexer (station identity as a single indexed categorical column, maxBins ≥ 91 so the tree can split on it) → VectorAssembler → GBT. Location is carried explicitly as lat/lon, so station is not one-hot encoded (which bloated the feature vector and memory).

Evaluation uses a temporal split — train on 2017–2023, test on 2024 — reflecting real forecasting (a random split would leak future information). Because rain is rare (train positive rate ≈ 1.9%), accuracy is uninformative (~0.98 by always predicting "no rain"); we therefore report AUC-ROC (ranking quality) and AUC-PR (the honest metric under heavy class imbalance), overall and per threshold.

5.4 Results

Full-data GBT (train 2017–2023, 8.0 M rows after a memory cap; test 2024, 1.59 M rows):

Metric AUC-ROC AUC-PR Accuracy F1
Overall 0.925 0.586 0.985 0.983

Per threshold, GBT vs a Logistic-Regression baseline:

Threshold (mm) GBT AUC-ROC GBT AUC-PR LogReg AUC-ROC LogReg AUC-PR
0.2 0.904 0.660 0.879 0.557
1.0 0.905 0.577 0.874 0.500
2.0 0.895 0.505 0.865 0.441
5.0 0.898 0.398 0.857 0.346
10.0 0.905 0.302 0.861 0.253

GBT beats the linear baseline at every threshold. AUC-ROC is stable (~0.90) while AUC-PR declines as the threshold rises — expected, since heavy-rain positives become progressively rarer.

5.5 Inference sanity check

Querying the saved model at real 2024 timestamps for station S77 confirms it is context-sensitive and uses the threshold correctly:

Context recent-30-min rain threshold P(> threshold)
Dry afternoon 0 mm 1.0 0.04
Heavy rain ongoing ≈46 mm 1.0 0.86
Heavy rain ongoing ≈46 mm 5.0 0.70

Dry inputs → ~4%; wet inputs → 70–86%; and at the same wet moment the probability correctly drops as the threshold rises. The trained pipeline is saved to models/rainfall_model/.

6. Additional study — model × compute benchmark

We extended Task 2 into a two-axis study. Model definitions (src/models/) and compute configurations (src/compute/) are modular registries, so one orchestrator (src/task2_train.py --model X --compute Y) runs any combination, logging train time, predict time, and AUC to CSV.

6.1 Model comparison (predictive error vs cost)

Eight models on their best configuration, ranked by AUC-PR:

Model Framework Train (s) Predict (s) AUC-ROC AUC-PR
GBT MLlib (CPU) 279 8.2 0.925 0.586
Random Forest MLlib (CPU) 173 8.4 0.902 0.560
MLP MLlib (CPU) 321 8.0 0.921 0.557
LSTM PyTorch (GPU) 75 0.4 0.915 0.476
TCN (1D-CNN) PyTorch (GPU) 80 0.4 0.915 0.473
Linear SVC MLlib (CPU) 44 5.4 0.875 0.468
Logistic Regression MLlib (CPU) 28 4.9 0.897 0.436
Factorization Machines MLlib (CPU) 278 5.5 0.814 0.196

  • GBT is best overall on both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR → the graded choice.
  • The non-linear models (GBT, MLP, RF) and the deep sequence models (LSTM, TCN) cluster at the top on AUC-ROC (~0.90–0.925); the linear models trail; Factorization Machines clearly underperform on this feature set.
  • The LSTM/TCN match the best MLlib models on AUC-ROC despite training on ~20× less data (400 k sampled rows vs 8 M, bounded by 4 GB VRAM) and are by far the fastest (train ~75–80 s, predict 0.4 s) — the best accuracy-per-compute. Their lower AUC-PR is largely a data-quantity artefact (see §7). MLlib was the required library, so GBT is the graded model and the deep models are a supplementary comparison; Spark MLlib has no recurrent model and is CPU-only, so the GPU cannot accelerate it.

6.2 Compute-configuration comparison (speed)

The four MLlib models were re-run across the five Spark configurations on an identical ~1 M-row sample so timing is comparable. Training time (s):

Config (cores) GBT RF LogReg LinSVC
local-all (16) 64 42 13 27
standalone-2×2 (4) 109 76 24 41
standalone-4×2 (8) 86 51 20 37
docker-2w (4) 102 72 22 46
docker-3w (6) 82 59 20 39

Findings (a textbook scale-out vs scale-up result):

  • local[*] is fastest — all 16 cores in one JVM, no network/serialization overhead.
  • Both cluster tiers are slower on a single machine, because distribution adds serialization/network/container overhead without adding hardware.
  • Within a cluster type, more workers = faster (standalone 2×2→4×2: 109→86 s; docker 2w→3w: 102→82 s for GBT) — real intra-cluster scale-out.
  • At equal worker counts, Docker ≈ Standalone — containerisation adds little beyond the distribution itself.
  • AUC is essentially identical across all configs (GBT ≈ 0.924 everywhere): the compute configuration changes speed, not predictive error.

Implication: on a single machine, more distribution adds overhead rather than speed; genuine training speed-up would require multiple physical nodes.

7. Limitations, observations, and insights

  • Observation — recent rain dominates. The 30-minute nowcast is driven mainly by the recent-rainfall features; the inference check (dry → 4%, wet → 86%) shows the model has learned rainfall's short-term persistence.
  • Observation — imbalance matters more than accuracy. With ~1.9% positives, accuracy is misleading; AUC-PR is the metric that actually separates the models and reveals the harder high-threshold cases.
  • Limitation — training-row cap. The threshold-as-feature design multiplies rows 5× (~240 M total); to fit GBT in 24 GB we cap training at ~8 M rows. Fewer thresholds or fewer features are local options to use more data.
  • Limitation — single machine. All compute tiers ran on one physical machine, so the cluster tiers demonstrate distributed deployment but cannot show true multi-node speed-up (which needs separate physical nodes). No cloud/HPC cluster was available.
  • Limitation — deep-model data parity. The LSTM/TCN trained on a 400 k-row GPU-memory-bounded sample, not the full data, so their AUC-PR is understated relative to the MLlib models; a larger GPU would allow a same-data comparison.
  • Insight / future work. A spatiotemporal model (ConvLSTM or graph-temporal network) ingesting all stations jointly could capture storm movement across the island; adding radar/reanalysis covariates and probability calibration would help operational use.

8. AI usage declaration

An AI coding assistant (within the Kiro IDE) was used, under the direction and review of the group members, to help: scaffold the PySpark pipeline and the modular model/compute registries; write and debug the cleaning, exploration, training, benchmark, and cluster-launch code; diagnose runtime issues (e.g. Python 3.12 distutils/numpy API changes, Spark executor-memory scheduling, Docker container networking); and draft this report and the project documentation. All modelling decisions, experiment design, executions on the group's hardware, and interpretation of results were directed and verified by the group members. Every number, table, and figure was produced by running the pipeline on the actual dataset; no results were fabricated by the AI.

9. Reproducibility

Full instructions are in README.md and RUNBOOK.md. In brief, from the project root:

python3 -m venv .venv && ./.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
./.venv/bin/python src/download_data.py            # 2017–2024 CSVs
./.venv/bin/python src/clean_data.py               # -> cleaned Parquet
./.venv/bin/python src/task1_explore.py            # Task 1 figures/tables
./.venv/bin/python src/task2_build_features.py     # Task 2 features
./.venv/bin/python src/task2_train.py --model gbt  # train + save GBT model
./.venv/bin/python src/task2_predict.py --station S77 --time "2024-06-15T14:00:00" --threshold 1.0

Benchmark study: src/benchmark.py (MLlib sweep), src/task2_deep.py (GPU LSTM/TCN), cluster/ (Spark Standalone), docker/ (Docker cluster), and src/benchmark_plot.py for the figures. Random seeds are fixed and the Spark session time zone is pinned to Asia/Singapore. The trained GBT pipeline is in models/rainfall_model/ (with model_metadata.json); the deep models are models/rainfall_lstm.pt and models/rainfall_tcn.pt.
